docs.text: HardFOC driver AT25040 Driver ¶ A header-only C++17 driver for the Microchip AT25040B serial EEPROM (also AT25010B and AT25020B). It detects the chip safely, reads and writes it in pages and reports every result as a status, on any MCU with SPI. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class with one method that runs an SPI transaction; it does the rest: the instruction set, the ninth address bit, bounds and page checks, and a probe that tells a missing chip from a present one. 4-Kbit SPI serial EEPROM AT25040B Microchip (Atmel) Memory 512 x 8 bits (AT25040B); 128 x 8 (AT25010B), 256 x 8 (AT25020B); 8-byte pages Interface SPI mode 0 or 3, MSB first; 20 MHz at 4.5 V to 5.5 V, 10 MHz at 2.5 V, 5 MHz at 1.8 V Supply 1.8 V to 5.5 V; 3.5 µA maximum standby at 5 V Writes Self-timed, 5 ms maximum per page; 1,000,000 cycles, 100-year retention Protection WP pin, write-enable latch, block protection of the top ¼, top ½ or whole array Package 8-lead SOIC, TSSOP, UDFN, XDFN, 8-ball VFBGA; -40 °C to +85 °C Product page and datasheet What you get ¶ One object per chip. at25040::Device<YourSpi> with Probe() , Read() , WritePage() , ReadStatus() and WriteEnable() . See API guide . Safe detection. Probe() reads the status register twice and rejects a floating bus ( 0xFF ) and a bus that echoes the command back. See Hardware . The ninth address bit handled. Addresses 0x100 to 0x1FF put A8 into the opcode for you. See Protocol . Checks before the bus. A bad pointer, a zero length, a range past the array or a write that crosses a page returns Status::Arg without touching SPI. Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class: no virtual calls, no heap, no exceptions, no RTOS. See Porting . Tested without hardware. Host unit tests run the driver against a model of the chip. See Testing and CI . docs.text: API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: detect the chip, read, write, wait, protect and handle errors. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with Eeprom standing for at25040::Device<MySpi> . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ One at25040::Device<Spi> object per chip, constructed from a reference to your port. It is not copyable and holds no buffers beyond the stack frame of each call. Call What it does Probe() Two RDSR: decides whether a chip is fitted ReadStatus(sr) One RDSR: write-cycle polling, protection level Read(addr, dst, len) One READ: up to 16 bytes from any address WritePage(addr, src, len) WREN + WRITE: 1 to 8 bytes in one page; starts a write cycle WriteEnable() One WREN, before an instruction you send yourself (WRSR) LastRdsr() No transfer: the last status byte read, for logging Every call except LastRdsr() returns at25040::Status and never throws. Check it. Detect the chip ¶ bool attach ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { switch ( eeprom . Probe ()) { case at25040 :: Status :: Ok : return true ; case at25040 :: Status :: Busy : // a write cycle is still running: try again in 5 ms case at25040 :: Status :: Absent : // no chip, floating MISO, MISO echoing MOSI, or a write cycle // (0xFF) default : std :: printf ( "no AT25040 (RDSR 0x%02X) \n " , eeprom . LastRdsr ()); return false ; } } Call Probe() from an explicit attach or start-up step, not from a static constructor: the SPI bus may not be up yet. A write cycle in progress also reads as Absent (every status bit is 1 while busy), so probe before you write, or wait 5 ms after the last write. Protocol lists every decision. Wait for a write cycle ¶ WritePage() returns as soon as the data is sent; the chip then needs up to 5 ms (t WC ) and ignores everything except RDSR until it is done. Poll the WIP bit: // Poll RDSR until the write cycle ends. tWC is 5 ms max; 100 x 100 us leaves a margin. at25040 :: Status wait_ready ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < 100 ; ++ i ) { uint8_t sr = 0xFF ; if ( eeprom . ReadStatus ( sr ) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return at25040 :: Status :: Timeout ; } if (( sr & at25040 :: kSrWip ) == 0 ) { return at25040 :: Status :: Ok ; } platform_delay_us ( 100 ); } return at25040 :: Status :: Busy ; } At 1 MHz one RDSR takes 16 µs on the bus, so a tight loop works too; the delay just keeps the bus free for other devices. Read ¶ // Read() moves at most 16 bytes per call, so read longer blocks in chunks. at25040 :: Status read_block ( Eeprom & eeprom , uint16_t addr , uint8_t * dst , uint16_t len ) { while ( len > 0 ) { const uint16_t n = len < 16 ? len : 16 ; const at25040 :: Status st = eeprom . Read ( addr , dst , n ); if ( st != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return st ; } addr = static_cast < uint16_t > ( addr + n ); dst += n ; len = static_cast < uint16_t > ( len - n ); } return at25040 :: Status :: Ok ; } Read() returns at most 16 bytes A longer len is shortened to 16 and the call still returns Ok . Read longer blocks in chunks, as above. Read() sets A8 in the opcode for addresses 0x100 and up, and refuses a range that runs past 0x1FF ( Status::Arg ). Write ¶ // WritePage() writes inside one 8-byte page. Split a longer write at page boundaries and wait after // each page. at25040 :: Status write_block ( Eeprom & eeprom , uint16_t addr , const uint8_t * src , uint16_t len ) { while ( len > 0 ) { const uint16_t room = static_cast < uint16_t > ( at25040 :: kPageSizeBytes - ( addr % at25040 :: kPageSizeBytes )); const uint16_t n = len < room ? len : room ; at25040 :: Status st = eeprom . WritePage ( addr , src , n ); if ( st == at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { st = wait_ready ( eeprom ); } if ( st != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return st ; } addr = static_cast < uint16_t > ( addr + n ); src += n ; len = static_cast < uint16_t > ( len - n ); } return at25040 :: Status :: Ok ; } A page is 8 bytes on an 8-byte boundary ( kPageSizeBytes ). WritePage() refuses a write that would cross one, because the chip would wrap inside the page and overwrite its start. Each page costs one write cycle, so writing the whole 512-byte array takes 64 cycles, at most 320 ms. Status and block protection ¶ void print_status ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { uint8_t sr = 0 ; if ( eeprom . ReadStatus ( sr ) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return ; } const unsigned bp = ( sr & ( at25040 :: kSrBp1 | at25040 :: kSrBp0 )) >> 2 ; // 0 none, 1 top 1/4, 2 top 1/2, 3 all std :: printf ( "busy=%d write-enabled=%d protect-level=%u \n " , ( sr & at25040 :: kSrWip ) != 0 , ( sr & at25040 :: kSrWel ) != 0 , bp ); } The driver does not wrap WRSR. Send it through your port after WriteEnable() : // Block protection (WRSR) is not wrapped by the driver: send it through your port. // level: 0 none, 1 = 0x180-0x1FF, 2 = 0x100-0x1FF, 3 = whole array. WP must be high. at25040 :: Status set_protection ( Eeprom & eeprom , MySpi & spi , uint8_t level ) { if ( level > 3 ) { return at25040 :: Status :: Arg ; } if ( eeprom . WriteEnable () != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return at25040 :: Status :: Timeout ; } const uint8_t tx [ 2 ] = { at25040 :: kCmdWrsr , static_cast < uint8_t > ( level << 2 )}; uint8_t rx [ 2 ] = {}; if ( ! spi . transfer ( tx , rx , sizeof ( tx ), 20 )) { return at25040 :: Status :: Timeout ; } return wait_ready ( eeprom ); // BP1/BP0 are non-volatile: a WRSR takes a write cycle } Level (BP1:BP0) Read-only addresses (AT25040B) 0 ( 00 ) None 1 ( 01 ) 0x180 - 0x1FF 2 ( 10 ) 0x100 - 0x1FF 3 ( 11 ) 0x000 - 0x1FF The bits are non-volatile. A write to a protected address is ignored by the chip and still returns Ok from WritePage() : read back what matters. Handle errors ¶ const char * describe ( at25040 :: Status st ) { switch ( st ) { case at25040 :: Status :: Ok : return "ok" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Timeout : return "SPI transfer failed" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Absent : return "no chip answered" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Busy : return "write cycle in progress" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Arg : return "bad pointer, length or address" ; } return "unknown" ; } Status Meaning Ok The transactions completed. It does not prove a write was stored Timeout Your port's transfer() returned false Absent Probe() only: no plausible status register ( Protocol ) Busy Probe() only: WIP set in a status byte that is not 0xFF Arg Read() , WritePage() : null pointer, zero length, range past the array, or a page crossing The chip itself reports nothing about a refused write (WP low, latch clear, protected block). The only check is to read the data back after the write cycle.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one call reaches the chip. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one at25040::Device object, whose public member functions (listed from inc/at25040.hpp) turn a call into AT25040 instructions: RDSR, WREN, READ and WRITE with A8 in the opcode. The communication interface (at25040::SpiInterface in inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP contract with one method. The platform port is the only code you write: a class whose transfer() runs one SPI transaction with chip select held low. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/at25040.hpp Device members ; inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer Where You change it Hardware-agnostic core : Device<Spi> , uses only the port's transfer() inc/at25040.hpp , inc/at25040_registers.hpp Never, for a new board Communication interface : SpiInterface<Derived> , one method inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp Never Platform port : your class, on your SDK Your project Once per MCU or board ( Porting ) Everything above the port is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the unit-test model. That is how the host tests run the real driver code without hardware. How one call reaches the chip ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant D as Device participant P as Your port participant E as AT25040B A->>D: WritePage(0x110, data, 4) D->>D: check pointer, length, page and range D->>P: transfer([0x06], 1 byte) P->>E: WREN D->>P: transfer([0x0A, 0x10, d0..d3], 6 bytes) P->>E: WRITE, A8 in the opcode P-->>D: true D-->>A: Status::Ok (write cycle now running in the chip) Each driver call is one or two transfer() calls; each transfer() is one CS-low period. The driver passes a 20 ms timeout to every transfer and never waits on its own. Why CRTP ¶ The interface is a class template parameter, not a virtual base class. The compiler sees your port's transfer() directly and inlines it; the driver has no vtable, allocates nothing and needs no RTTI. The cost is that the driver type names the port: Device<MySpi> . Code that has to work with several port types takes the driver as a template parameter too. No hidden waits, no hidden state ¶ The driver keeps one byte of state: the last status register value ( LastRdsr() ). It does not track the write cycle, the write-enable latch or the protection level; the chip does, and ReadStatus() reads them. That keeps every call's cost visible: one call, at most two transactions, no delay. docs.text: Configuration ¶ What you choose for an AT25040B: the part, the bus, write protection and the driver's fixed limits. The driver has no run-time configuration structure. Everything below is a board decision, a compile-time constant in inc/at25040_registers.hpp or a value in the chip's status register. docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and an AT25040B, with which bus settings, and the board-level details that decide whether writes stick. All values here come from the AT25010B/AT25020B/AT25040B datasheet (Atmel-8707F, 01/2015). When they disagree with a board's schematic, the schematic wins for pin numbers. Pins ¶ The 8-lead SOIC and TSSOP use the same pin numbers; the 8-pad UDFN / XDFN and the 8-ball VFBGA number the same functions 1 to 8. Pin Signal Notes 1 CS, in Active low; each instruction starts on its falling edge 2 SO, out MISO; high impedance while CS is high 3 WP, in Active low; low blocks every write 4 GND 5 SI, in MOSI 6 SCK, in Clock 7 HOLD, in Active low; pauses a transfer 8 VCC 1.8 V to 5.5 V The driver does not drive WP or HOLD. Tie HOLD high. Tie WP high to allow writes, or drive it from a GPIO and hold it low to make the whole chip read-only in hardware. Bus settings ¶ Setting Value Mode 0 or 3, MSB first f SCK max 20 MHz (VCC ≥ 4.5 V), 10 MHz (≥ 2.5 V), 5 MHz (≥ 1.8 V) t CSS , t CSH , t CS min 100 ns (VCC ≥ 2.5 V), 200 ns (≥ 1.8 V) Frame Instruction, address (READ, WRITE), data; no dummy bytes t WC max 5 ms, self-timed, from the CS rising edge t CSS is CS setup before the first clock, t CSH CS hold after the last, t CS the CS high time between instructions. sequenceDiagram participant H as Host (driver) participant E as AT25040B H->>E: WREN 0x06 (CS low, 1 byte, CS high) H->>E: WRITE 0x0A (A8 = 1), address byte 0x10, 4 data bytes: address 0x110 Note over E: CS high: internal write cycle starts, 5 ms max H->>E: RDSR 0x05 E-->>H: 0xFF (busy: every status bit reads 1) H->>E: RDSR 0x05 E-->>H: 0x00 (ready, write-enable latch cleared) H->>E: READ 0x0B (A8 = 1), address byte 0x10 E-->>H: 4 data bytes The opcode carries the ninth address bit (A8) in bit 3 for READ and WRITE on the AT25040B. The driver sets it for addresses 0x100 to 0x1FF . Protocol has every instruction and the status register. Power ¶ Quantity Value VCC 1.8 V to 5.5 V; the clock limit depends on it Active current (5 V) 10 mA max at 20 MHz (read), 3 mA max at 1 MHz Standby current (max, CS high) 0.5 µA at 1.8 V, 1 µA at 2.5 V, 3.5 µA at 5 V Temperature -40 °C to +85 °C (industrial grade, H) Match VCC to the MCU's I/O voltage: the inputs need V IH of at least 0.7 x VCC. Decouple VCC with 100 nF close to pin 8. Write protection ¶ Three mechanisms stop a write; all of them make WritePage() look successful while nothing is stored, because the chip does not report a refused write. Mechanism Effect WP pin low (board) Every write and WREN is ignored Write-enable latch clear (power-up, WRDI, end of every write cycle) The next WRITE is ignored; WritePage() sends WREN first Block protection BP1:BP0 (WRSR, non-volatile) 01 : 0x180 - 0x1FF , 10 : 0x100 - 0x1FF , 11 : all read-only API guide shows how to read and set the protection level. Sharing the bus ¶ SO is high impedance whenever CS is high, so the AT25040B can share SCK, MOSI and MISO with other SPI devices on its own chip select. On the Flux analog front-end it sits on the ADS7952 bus as the second device. Variants ¶ Part Size Protected by BP = 01 / 10 AT25010B 128 x 8 0x60 - 0x7F / 0x40 - 0x7F AT25020B 256 x 8 0xC0 - 0xFF / 0x80 - 0xFF AT25040B 512 x 8, A8 in the opcode 0x180 - 0x1FF / 0x100 - 0x1FF BP = 11 protects the whole array on every part. The driver checks addresses against 512 bytes ( kCapacityBytes ). On the smaller parts, keep addresses below 128 or 256 yourself: the chip ignores the upper address bits, so higher addresses alias the start of the array. docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++17 library with no dependencies. Requirements ¶ A C++17 compiler: GCC 7+, Clang 5+ or a current MSVC. No RTOS, heap or exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns at25040::Status . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-at25040-driver.git external/hf-at25040-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-at25040-driver Only inc/ , cmake/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples have their own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ); you do not need it to use the driver. CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-at25040-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf_at25040 ) # or the alias hf::at25040 hf_at25040 is an INTERFACE target: it carries the include directories ( inc/ and the generated version header) and requires C++17 ( cxx_std_17 ), so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect HF_AT25040_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host unit tests and the documentation snippets in tests/ ( Testing and CI ) Without CMake, add inc/ to the include path. at25040.hpp then falls back to a built-in version string. ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF component wrapper is examples/esp32/components/hf_at25040/ . Copy that folder into your project's components/ (or point EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at it) and set the HF_AT25040_ROOT cache variable to the driver checkout; the wrapper stops with a clear message when the path is wrong. Your component then declares REQUIRES hf_at25040 . Inside hf-core ¶ In the HardFOC core, the driver is a submodule of hf-core-drivers and is switched on with HF_CORE_ENABLE_AT25040 , which also compiles the At25040Handler : set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_AT25040 ON ) include ( "${HF_CORE_DRIVER_EXT}/hf-at25040-driver/cmake/hf_at25040_build_settings.cmake" ) How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/hf_at25040_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target for host builds and CI ESP-IDF examples/esp32/components/hf_at25040/CMakeLists.txt IDF component wrapper over the same settings The version is set once in the settings file and written into at25040_version.h at configure time. Read it at run time: const char * v = at25040 :: GetAt25040DriverVersion (); // "1.0.0" Next ¶ Quickstart wires the chip and stores a few bytes; Porting writes the SPI interface for your MCU.

docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class with one method: the SPI transfer. The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls transfer() on a class you derive from at25040::SpiInterface<Self> (in inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp ). The base class uses CRTP: the call is resolved at compile time, so there are no virtual functions, no vtable and nothing to allocate. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one at25040::Device object, whose public member functions (listed from inc/at25040.hpp) turn a call into AT25040 instructions: RDSR, WREN, READ and WRITE with A8 in the opcode. The communication interface (at25040::SpiInterface in inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP contract with one method. The platform port is the only code you write: a class whose transfer() runs one SPI transaction with chip select held low. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/at25040.hpp Device members ; inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ bool transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len , uint32_t timeout_ms ); Argument Contract tx , len Send len bytes in one transaction, CS low for all of them rx Receive len bytes: rx[i] is the byte clocked in while tx[i] went out timeout_ms Give up after this long and return false return true when the transaction completed, false on a bus error or timeout The driver always passes rx of the same length as tx (at most 18 bytes) and timeout_ms = 20 . SPI port ¶ my_spi.hpp #include "at25040_spi_interface.hpp" class MySpi : public at25040 :: SpiInterface < MySpi > { public : // One transaction: CS low, `len` bytes full duplex (SPI mode 0 or 3, MSB first), CS high. // rx[i] is the byte clocked in while tx[i] went out. Return false only on a bus error or timeout. bool transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len , uint32_t timeout_ms ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len , timeout_ms ); } }; Rules the transfer must follow: SPI mode 0 or 3 , MSB first, no faster than the chip allows at your VCC: 20 MHz at 4.5 V, 10 MHz at 2.5 V, 5 MHz at 1.8 V. One transaction per call. CS goes low before the first byte and high after the last; never split a call into two CS periods, never merge two calls. The chip starts a write cycle on the CS rising edge after WRITE. Full duplex. Fill rx with what came back on MISO; Probe() and Read() read their results from it. Return false only for a bus failure. A missing chip is the driver's job: it shows up as 0xFF bytes. Chip select and shared buses ¶ Drive CS from the SPI peripheral (ESP-IDF spics_io_num , STM32 hardware NSS) or toggle a GPIO around the transfer. On a shared bus, take the bus lock for the whole transfer() so another device cannot get between CS low and CS high. Keep t CSS , t CSH and t CS at 100 ns or more (200 ns at 1.8 V). Reference implementation ¶ The ESP32 example's port in at25040_esp32_example.cpp is a skeleton: its transfer() returns false until you connect it to spi_device_transmit() for your board. With ESP-IDF's spi_master , one spi_transaction_t with length = len * 8 , tx_buffer = tx and rx_buffer = rx on a device configured for mode 0 is the whole port. Check your port ¶ Build it: the port on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over it. Call Probe() and log LastRdsr() . A ready AT25040B with no protection reads 0x00 ; 0xFF means nothing answered. Write one page, wait for WIP to clear, read it back. Read across 0x0FF / 0x100 in two calls to prove A8 reaches the chip: the two halves must hold different data. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each EEPROM one owner task, or guard every call on a driver object (and its port) with one mutex. On a shared bus, the bus lock in transfer() is not enough for a write followed by a status poll; hold the mutex for the whole sequence.

docs.text: Protocol ¶ The AT25040B's instruction set, status register and addressing, and which driver call uses each instruction. Every instruction starts with CS going low and ends with CS going high. Bytes go MSB first. An invalid opcode leaves SO in high impedance until the next CS falling edge. Instructions ¶ Instruction Opcode What it does WREN 0x06 Sets the write-enable latch; WP must be high. WriteEnable() , WritePage() WRDI 0x04 Clears the write-enable latch. Not wrapped RDSR 0x05 Reads the status register, also during a write cycle. ReadStatus() , Probe() WRSR 0x01 Writes BP1:BP0 (non-volatile, takes a write cycle). Not wrapped READ 0x03 , 0x0B with A8 Address byte, then data out; the address increments. Read() WRITE 0x02 , 0x0A with A8 Address byte, then 1 to 8 data bytes in one page. WritePage() The datasheet writes the opcodes as 0000 X110 (WREN) to 0000 A010 (WRITE); the constants are kCmdWren , kCmdWrdi , kCmdRdsr , kCmdWrsr , kCmdRead and kCmdWrite . A is address bit A8 on the AT25040B ( kAddrA8Mask = 0x08 ); X is ignored. During a write cycle every instruction except RDSR is ignored. Status register ¶ Bit Name Meaning 0 RDY ( kSrWip ) 1: write cycle in progress 1 WEN ( kSrWel ) 1: write-enable latch set 2 BP0 ( kSrBp0 ) Block protection, low bit 3 BP1 ( kSrBp1 ) Block protection, high bit 7:4 0 when ready During an internal write cycle all eight bits read 1, so a busy chip returns 0xFF . A ready chip returns 0x0X : only the low four bits can be set. Addressing and wrap-around ¶ READ : the address increments after each byte and rolls over from 0x1FF to 0x000 . WRITE : only the low three address bits increment, so a write wraps inside its 8-byte page and overwrites the start of the page. The driver never lets either wrap happen: Read() refuses a range past 0x1FF , WritePage() refuses a write that crosses a page, both with Status::Arg . Probe ¶ Probe() sends RDSR twice and decides from the two status bytes: Status bytes Result Typical cause A transfer failed Absent Bus error in the port The two bytes differ Absent Noise, a contended MISO 0xFF Absent Nothing drives MISO (pull-up or floating), or a write cycle is running 0x05 Absent MISO follows MOSI one byte late: the RDSR opcode comes back WIP set, not 0xFF Busy Not seen on an AT25040B, which reads 0xFF while busy Anything else Ok A ready chip: 0x00 to 0x0E LastRdsr() returns the first status byte of the last probe, for logging.

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Store four bytes in an AT25040B and read them back: wire six signals, write a one-method port class, call four driver functions. 1. Wire it ¶ MCU AT25040B pin Notes SPI SCLK SCK (6) Mode 0 or 3; start at 1 MHz SPI MOSI SI (5) SPI MISO SO (2) High impedance while CS is high GPIO or hardware CS CS (1) Active low; one transaction per CS-low period 3.3 V (1.8 V to 5.5 V) VCC (8) Decouple with 100 nF close to the pin 3.3 V or GPIO WP (3) High to allow writes; low blocks every write 3.3 V HOLD (7) Keep high unless you pause transfers GND GND (4) Common ground with the MCU The Hardware page has the bus timing, the other packages and the protection options. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the hf_at25040 CMake target (or add inc/ to your include path and build with C++17). Installation covers CMake and ESP-IDF. git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-at25040-driver.git external/hf-at25040-driver 3. Write the port ¶ The port is the only platform code: one method that runs one SPI transaction. Replace the platform_* call with your SDK's. my_spi.hpp #include "at25040_spi_interface.hpp" class MySpi : public at25040 :: SpiInterface < MySpi > { public : // One transaction: CS low, `len` bytes full duplex (SPI mode 0 or 3, MSB first), CS high. // rx[i] is the byte clocked in while tx[i] went out. Return false only on a bus error or timeout. bool transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len , uint32_t timeout_ms ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len , timeout_ms ); } }; Porting explains the contract and shows how to check a port. 4. Store and read back ¶ main.cpp #include "at25040.hpp" int store_and_read_back ( MySpi & spi ) { at25040 :: Device < MySpi > eeprom ( spi ); if ( eeprom . Probe () != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { // 1. a chip is there and idle return -1 ; // wiring, CS, power or SPI mode } const uint8_t serial [ 4 ] = { 0x12 , 0x34 , 0x56 , 0x78 }; if ( eeprom . WritePage ( 0x010 , serial , sizeof ( serial )) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { // 2. one page return -2 ; } uint8_t sr = 0xFF ; // 3. wait for the write cycle (5 ms max) for ( int i = 0 ; i < 100 && ( sr & at25040 :: kSrWip ) != 0 ; ++ i ) { platform_delay_us ( 100 ); if ( eeprom . ReadStatus ( sr ) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return -3 ; } } uint8_t back [ 4 ] = {}; // 4. read it back if ( eeprom . Read ( 0x010 , back , sizeof ( back )) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return -4 ; } return back [ 0 ] == serial [ 0 ] ? 0 : -5 ; } What each step does: Probe() reads the status register twice. It returns Ok only when both reads agree, look like a real status byte and show no write in progress. WritePage() sends WREN, then WRITE with the address and up to eight bytes inside one page. The chip starts its internal write cycle when CS goes high. The loop polls the status register until bit 0 (WIP) clears. The driver does not wait for you: a read or a second write during the write cycle is ignored by the chip. Read() sends READ and the address and returns up to 16 bytes per call. platform_delay_us() stands for your SDK's microsecond delay. This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. If it does not work ¶ Symptom First thing to check Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0xFF MISO wiring, CS reaching pin 1, VCC; a write cycle still running Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0x05 MISO is connected to MOSI, or the wrong CS is low Writes return Ok but the data does not change WP is low, the address is block-protected, or you read before the write cycle ended Data at 0x100 and up appears at 0x000 The part is an AT25010B or AT25020B, not an AT25040B Troubleshooting has the full list. docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host unit tests against a model of the chip, compiled documentation, ESP32 builds and static analysis, on every pull request. Host unit tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a model of the AT25040B on the SPI bus: the instruction set with A8 in the opcode, the write-enable latch, page wrap-around, block protection, and a write cycle during which the status register reads 0xFF . The bus can also float, echo MOSI or fail. cmake -S . -B build-host -DHF_AT25040_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build-host ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_device.cpp Probe decisions, A8 placement, argument checks, the 16-byte read limit, page writes and the write cycle tests/mock_at25040.hpp The chip model Documentation snippets ¶ Every C++ block on this site is included from tests/docs/ , which the host build compiles (target hf_at25040_doc_snippets ) with the driver instantiated over the documented port. A change to the API that breaks a page breaks the build first. CI workflows ¶ Workflow What it checks Host unit tests GCC and Clang build and run the tests and the doc snippets ESP32 examples build Every app in examples/esp32/app_config.yml , for each listed ESP-IDF version and build type C++ lint, C++ analysis clang-format, clang-tidy and cppcheck Docs Strict site build, figure and generated-table drift, Doxygen, link check, Lighthouse budget Markdown lint, YAML lint, link check Repository text files The workflows call the shared, versioned workflows of hf-general-ci-tools and hf-espidf-ci-tools . docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up an AT25040B, their causes and the fix for each. Start with LastRdsr() after a failed Probe() : it tells a dead bus ( 0xFF ), a looped-back bus ( 0x05 ) and a working chip apart without a logic analyser. Symptom Cause and fix Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0xFF Nothing drives MISO: wiring, CS on the wrong pin, no VCC. Fix: Check SO (pin 2) to MISO, CS (pin 1), VCC (pin 8) Same, right after a write The chip is in its write cycle: all status bits read 1. Fix: Wait 5 ms after the last write, or poll ReadStatus() before probing Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0x05 MISO echoes MOSI one byte late. Fix: Look for a short between SI and SO, or a missing device on that CS Probe() returns Absent , the two reads differ Bus contention or noise. Fix: Another device drives MISO while this CS is low; lower the clock Every call returns Timeout Your port's transfer() returned false . Fix: Bus not initialised, or the bus lock timed out WritePage() returns Ok , data unchanged WP low, the address is block-protected, or you read before the write cycle ended. Fix: WP (pin 3) high; ReadStatus() BP bits; wait for WIP to clear Only the first write of a burst sticks Writes sent during the previous write cycle are ignored. Fix: Wait for WIP after each WritePage() ( API guide ) WritePage() returns Arg More than 8 bytes, or the write crosses an 8-byte page. Fix: Split at page boundaries ( API guide ) A long read returns only part of the data Read() moves at most 16 bytes per call and still returns Ok . Fix: Read in chunks of 16 Data at 0x100 and up appears at 0x000 An AT25010B or AT25020B: no A8. Fix: Check the part marking; keep to its size Reads fine, writes fail at high clock Clock above the limit for your VCC. Fix: 5 MHz at 1.8 V, 10 MHz at 2.5 V, 20 MHz at 4.5 V Random failures, worse with long wires HOLD floating. Fix: Tie HOLD (pin 7) high
